'''Pamela Ann Silver''' is an American [[biologist]], [[Biological engineering|bioengineer]] and professor. She is the Elliot T. and Onie H. Adams Professorship of Biochemistry and Systems Biology at [[Harvard Medical School]].<ref name="gs">{{Google scholar id}}</ref><ref name="epmc">{{EuropePMC}}</ref> Silver is one of the founding Core Faculty Members of the [[Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering]] at [[Harvard University]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20100906100857/http://wyss.harvard.edu/viewpage/128/pamela-silver Silver profile page, Wyss Institute]</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20050905082003/http://sysbio.med.harvard.edu/phd/index.html Systems Biology PhD Program]</ref>

She has made contributions to the fields of [[Cell (biology)|cell]] and nuclear biology,<ref>{{cite journal|author=Jason A Kahana|author2=Bruce J Schnapp|author3=Pamela A Silver|title=Kinetics of spindle pole body separation in budding yeast|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=October 10, Silver was the first director of the Harvard University Graduate Program in Systems Biology.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Systems, Synthetic, and Quantitative Biology | url=http://sysbiophd.harvard.edu | access-date=2024-12-27 | website=sysbiophd.harvard.edu}}</ref> She serves as a member of the National Science Advisory Board for [[Biosecurity]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity (NSABB)|url=https://osp.od.nih.gov/biotechnology/national-science-advisory-board-for-biosecurity-nsabb/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171228163549/https://osp.od.nih.gov/biotechnology/national-science-advisory-board-for-biosecurity-nsabb/|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 28, 2017|access-date=2021-01-16|website=Office of Science Policy|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Silver grew up in [[Atherton, California]], where she attended Laurel and Encinal Elementary Schools.  During this time, she was a winner of the [[IBM]] Math Competition, winning a slide rule,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2017/05/harvards-pamela-silver-recalls-journey-from-silicon-valley-to-synthetic-biology/|title=Harvard's Pamela Silver recalls journey from Silicon Valley to synthetic biology|date=2017-05-16|website=Harvard Gazette|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> and received special recognition for her early aptitude in science.  She attended [[Menlo-Atherton High School]] and graduated from [[Castilleja School]] in Palo Alto.  She received her B.A. in chemistry from the [[University of California, Santa Cruz]] and her PhD in Biological Chemistry from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] in 1982 in the laboratory of [[William T. Wickner]], working largely on the coat assembly of the M13 [[coliphage]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Silver|first1=P.|last2=Watts|first2=C.|last3=Wickner|first3=W.|date=August 1981|title=Membrane assembly from purified components. I. Isolated M13 procoat does not require ribosomes or soluble proteins for processing by membranes|journal=Cell|volume=25|issue=2|pages=341–345|issn=0092-8674|pmid=7026042|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(81)90052-0|s2cid=24764847}}</ref><ref name=phd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|first=Pamela Ann|last=Silver|oclc=763038710|title      = Mechanisms of membrane assembly : studies on the association of an integral protein with biological membranes|id={{ProQuest|303201897}}|publisher=University of California, Los Angeles|year=1982}}</ref>

==Career==
Silver did her [[postdoctoral research]] with [[Mark Ptashne]] at [[Harvard University]] where she discovered one of the first nuclear localization sequences.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Silver, P. | author2=Keegan, L. | author3=Ptashne, M. | name-list-style=amp |title=The amino terminus of the yeast GAL4 gene product is sufficient for nuclear localization | journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA  |year=1984 |volume=81 | issue=19 |pages=5951–5 |doi=10.1073/pnas.81.19.5951 |pmid=6091123 | pmc=391836| bibcode=1984PNAS...81.5951S | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=Silver, P. | author2=Chiang, A. | author3=Sadler, I. | name-list-style=amp  |title=Mutations affecting localization and production of a yeast nuclear protein | journal=Genes & Development |year=1988  |volume=2 | issue=6 |pages=707–17|doi=10.1101/gad.2.6.707 | pmid=3138162 | doi-access=free }}</ref> She continued to study the mechanism of nuclear localization in her own lab as an assistant professor at [[Princeton University]]. During this time, she characterized the receptor for NLSs and discovered one of the first eukaryotic DnaJ chaperones.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Blumberg, H.  |author2=Silver, P.    |name-list-style=amp | title=SCJ1, a DNAJ homologue that alters protein sorting in yeast   | journal=Nature  |year=1991  |volume=349 |issue=6310    |pages=627–30 | doi=10.1038/349627a0 | pmid=2000136|s2cid=4358892 }}</ref>

Silver continued in the area of Cell Biology upon moving to the [[Dana Farber Cancer Institute]] to hold the Claudia Adams Barr Investigatorship and to become Associate Professor of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology at Harvard Medical School and Dana-Farber.  During this time, she was among the first to follow GFP-tagged proteins in living cells.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Kahana, J. | author2=Schnapp, B. | author3=Silver, P. | name-list-style=amp  | title=Kinetics of spindle pole body separation in budding yeast | journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. |year=1995 |volume=92 | issue=21 |pages=9707–9711 | doi=10.1073/pnas.92.21.9707 | pmid=7568202 | pmc=40871| bibcode=1995PNAS...92.9707K | doi-access=free }}</ref> In addition, she initiated early studies in systems biology to examine interactions within the nucleus on a whole genome scale.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Casolari, J. | author2=Brown, CR | author3=Komili, S. | author4=West, J. | author5=Hieronymus, H. | author6=Silver, PA. | name-list-style=amp | title=Genome-wide localization of the nuclear transport machinery reveals coupling of transcriptional status and nuclear organization  |year=2004  | journal=Cell |volume=117 | issue=4 |pages=427–439 | doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(04)00448-9 | pmid=15137937| s2cid=8932425 | doi-access=free }}</ref>  Together with Bill Sellers, she discovered molecules that block nuclear export<ref>{{cite journal | author=Kau, TR | author2=Schroeder, F | author3=Wojciechowski, C. | author4=Zhou, JJ | author5=Roberts, T. | author6=Clardy, J | author7=Sellers, W | author8=Silver, PA. | name-list-style=amp  | title=A chemical genetic screen for inhibitors of regulated export of a Forkhead transcription factor in tumor cells |year=2003  | journal=Cancer Cell |volume=4  | issue=6 |pages=463–476|doi=10.1016/s1535-6108(03)00303-9 | pmid=14706338 | doi-access=free }}</ref> and formed the basis for a publicly traded company Karyopharm Therapeutics.  She was promoted in 1997 to Professor of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology at Harvard Medical School and Dana-Farber.

In 2004, Silver moved to the newly formed Department of Systems Biology at [[Harvard Medical School]] as a Professor.  Around this time, she worked closely with the Synthetic Biology Working Group at MIT and made the decision to move her research group into [[Synthetic Biology]].  She observed the motion of the carbon fixing organelles in photosynthetic bacteria.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Savage D, Afonso B, Silver PA | title=Spatially ordered dynamics of the bacterial carbon fixation machinery |year=2010 | journal=Science |volume=327 | issue=5970 |pages=1258–61|doi=10.1126/science.1186090 |pmid=20203050| bibcode=2010Sci...327.1258S | s2cid=36685539 }}</ref>  She has worked extensively on designing modified bacteria to act as sensors for exposure to a drug<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Kotula JW, Kerns SJ, Shaket LA, Siraj L, Collins JJ, Way JC, SIlver PA|date=April 1, 2014|title=Programmable bacteria detect and record an environmental signal in the mammalian gut|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=111|issue=13|pages=4838–4843|doi=10.1073/pnas.1321321111|pmc=3977281|pmid=24639514|bibcode=2014PNAS..111.4838K|doi-access=free}}</ref> or inflammation<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Riglar|first1=David T.|last2=Giessen|first2=Tobias W.|last3=Baym|first3=Michael|last4=Kerns|first4=S. Jordan|last5=Niederhuber|first5=Matthew J.|last6=Bronson|first6=Roderick T.|last7=Kotula|first7=Jonathan W.|last8=Gerber|first8=Georg K.|last9=Way|first9=Jeffrey C.|date=July 2017|title=Engineered bacteria can function in the mammalian gut long-term as live diagnostics of inflammation|journal=Nature Biotechnology|volume=35|issue=7|pages=653–658|doi=10.1038/nbt.3879|issn=1546-1696|pmc=5658125|pmid=28553941}}</ref> in the mammalian gut. She has served as the Director of an ARPA-E (DOE) project on [[electrofuel]]s.

Her former students include [[Christina Agapakis]],<ref name=agaphd/> [[Valerie Weiss]], [[Karmella Haynes]], [[Jessica Polka]] and [[Anita Corbett]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Nature Awards give mentors the recognition, funding, and 'street cred' they need |author=Anon|year=2019 |url=https://www.springernature.com/gp/researchers/the-source/blog/blogposts-life-in-research/nature-award-mentoring-science-corbett/17283086 |access-date=2023-05-02 |website=springernature.com}}</ref>

==Research==
===Synthetic Biology===
Some of Silver's work in this area includes the engineering of: mammalian cells to remember and report past exposures to drugs and radiation,<ref>{{cite journal|author=Ajo-Franklin, CM|author2=Drubin, DA|author3=Eskin, J.|author4=Gee, E.|author5=Landgraf, D.|author6=Philips, I.|author7=Silver, PA.|name-list-style=amp|title=Rational design of memory in eukaryotic cells|journal=Genes & Development|date=September 15, 2007|volume=21|issue=18|pages=2271–2276|pmid=17875664|doi=10.1101/gad.1586107|pmc=1973140}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Burrill D, Silver PA|name-list-style=amp|title=Synthetic circuit identifies sub-populations with sustained memory of DNA damage|journal=Genes & Development|date=2011|volume=25|issue=5|pages=434–439|doi=10.1101/gad.1994911|pmc=3049284|pmid=21363961}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Burrill DR, Inniss MC, Boyle PM, Silver PA|name-list-style=amp|title=Synthetic memory circuits for tracking human cell fate|journal=Genes & Development|date=July 1, 2012|volume=26|issue=13|pages=1486–1497|pmid=22751502|doi=10.1101/gad.189035.112|pmc=3403016}}</ref> robust computational circuits in embryonic stem cells and bacteria,<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Robinson-Mosher A, Chen JH, Way J, Silver PA|title=Designing cell-targeted therapeutic proteins reveals the interplay between domain connectivity and cell binding|journal=Biophysical Journal|date=November 18, 2014|volume=107|issue=10|pages=2456–2466|doi=10.1016/j.bpj.2014.10.007|pmid=25418314|pmc=4241446|bibcode=2014BpJ...107.2456R}}</ref> and synthetic switches to moderate [[gene silencing]] with the integration of novel therapeutic proteins.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Haynes KA, Silver PA|title=Synthetic reversal of epigenetic silencing|journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry|date=August 5, 2011|volume=286|issue=31|pages=27176–27182|doi=10.1074/jbc.C111.229567|pmid=21669865|pmc=3149311|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Alexander A. Green|author2=Pamela A. Silver|author3=James J. Collins|author4=Peng Yin|name-list-style=amp|title=Toehold Switches: De-Novo-Designed Regulators of Gene Expression|journal=Cell|date=November 6, 2014|volume=159|issue=4|pages=925–39|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2014.10.002|url=https://yin.hms.harvard.edu/publications/2014.tswitch.pdf|accessdate=7 May 2015|pmid=25417166|pmc=4265554}}</ref> Silver's work sets the stage for the development of novel therapies for use in both humans and animals.

===Carbon fixation and sustainability===
Silver has characterized the carboxysome – the major carbon-fixing structure in cyanobacteria – to enhance photosynthetic efficiency<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Ducat DC, Avelar-Rivas JA, Way JC, Silver PA|title=Rerouting carbon flux to enhance photosynthetic productivity|journal=Applied and Environmental Microbiology|date=April 2012|volume=78|issue=8|pages=2660–2668|doi=10.1128/AEM.07901-11|pmid=22307292|pmc=3318813|bibcode=2012ApEnM..78.2660D}}</ref> and carbon fixation.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Ducat DC, Silver PA|title=Improving carbon pathways|journal=Current Opinion in Chemical Biology|date=August 2012|volume=16|issue=3–4|pages=337–344|doi=10.1016/j.cbpa.2012.05.002|pmid=22647231|pmc=3424341}}</ref> She has also engineered cyanobacteria to more efficiently cycle carbon into high-value commodities and has shown that these bacteria can form sustainable consortia.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Polka J, Silver PA|title=Building synthetic cellular organization|journal=Molecular Biology of the Cell|date=December 1, 2013|volume=24|issue=23|pages=3585–3587|doi=10.1091/mbc.E13-03-0155|pmc=3842987|pmid=24288075}}</ref> In a collaboration with [[Jessica Polka]], Silver performed [[super-resolution microscopy]] of the β-carboxysome.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Niederhuber|first1=Matthew J.|last2=Lambert|first2=Talley J.|last3=Yapp|first3=Clarence|last4=Silver|first4=Pamela A.|last5=Polka|first5=Jessica K.|date=2017-10-01|title=Superresolution microscopy of the β-carboxysome reveals a homogeneous matrix|journal=Molecular Biology of the Cell|volume=28|issue=20|pages=2734–2745|doi=10.1091/mbc.E17-01-0069|issn=1939-4586|pmc=5620380|pmid=28963440}}</ref>

[[File:Bionic leaf.png|thumb|The bionic leaf is a system for converting solar energy into liquid fuel developed by the labs of Daniel Nocera and Pamela Silver at Harvard.]]
Silver collaborated with [[Daniel Nocera]] at Harvard University to develop a device, called the "[[Bionic Leaf]]", that converts solar energy into fuel through a hybrid water-splitting catalyst system that leverages metabolically engineered bacteria.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Torella JP, Gagliardi CJ, Chen JS, Bediako DK, Colon B, Way JC, SIlver PA, Nocera DG|title=Efficient solar-to-fuels production from a hybrid microbial-water-splitting catalyst system|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=February 24, 2015|volume=112|issue=8|pages=2337–2342|doi=10.1073/pnas.1424872112|pmid=25675518|pmc=4345567|bibcode=2015PNAS..112.2337T|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Gene regulation===
Silver discovered a correlation between nuclear transport and gene regulation – she identified the first arginine methyltransferase, which plays a role in chromatin function and is important to the movement of RNA binding proteins between the nucleus and cytoplasm of cells. She also discovered previously unknown variations among ribosomes that led her to propose a unique specificity for the matching between ribosomes and the subsequent translation of mRNAs. Silver's finding has several implications for our understanding of how gene regulation impacts disease development, such as cancer.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Yu MC, Lamming DW, Eskin JA, Sinclair DA, Silver PA|name-list-style=amp|title=The role of arginine methylation in formation of silent chromatin|journal=Genes & Development|date=December 1, 2006|volume=20|issue=23|pages=3249–3254|pmid=17158743|doi=10.1101/gad.1495206|pmc=1686602}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Silver has been the recipient of an NSF [[Presidential Young Investigator Award]], a Basil O’Connor Research Scholar of the March of Dimes, an Established Investigator of the American Heart Association, the NIH Directors Lecture, and NIH MERIT award, Innovation award at BIO,  a Fellow of the [[Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study]], the Elliot T. and Onie H. Adams Professorship at Harvard Medical School and named the Top 20 Global Synthetic Biology Influencers.  She sits on numerous advisory boards and has presented to members of the US Congress.

Silver was awarded the BBS Mentoring Award for Graduate Education at Harvard Medical School.  She is also one of the founders of the [[International Genetically Engineered Machine|International Genetically Engineered Machines]] competition (iGEM) and currently sits on the Board of iGEM.org.  Silver founded and was the first Director of the Harvard University Graduate Program in Systems Biology. Silver was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2017<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/content/members/newFellows.aspx?s=a|title=Newly Elected Fellows|website=www.amacad.org|access-date=2017-05-01}}</ref> and the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2023.
